title: Whom Do You Seek?
paragraphs:
Whom Do You Seek?
The Question That Exposes Every Heart and Changes Every Life
There are questions that inform us.
There are questions that challenge us.
And then there are questions that uncover us.
At first glance, it sounds simple. Ordinary. Almost casual.
But Scripture reveals that this question is anything but ordinary.
A question that has echoed through gardens, deserts, crowded streets, empty tombs, and broken hearts for thousands of years.
A question that still follows every human soul today.
Because beneath every ambition, every addiction, every success, every failure, every relationship, every disappointment, and every hidden longing lies a deeper pursuit.
Whether they realize it or not.
The tragedy is that many spend their entire lives seeking everything except the One they were created to seek.
The question appears powerfully in John 20.
The crucifixion had shattered the hopes of Jesus' followers.
And Mary Magdalene stood outside an empty tomb weeping.
"They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid Him."
Then Jesus Himself stood before her, though she did not recognize Him.
"Γύναι, τί κλαίεις; τίνα ζητεῖς;" (Gynai, ti klaieis? Tina zēteis?)
"Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?" (John 20:15)
Notice what Jesus did not ask.
He did not ask about her theology.
He did not ask about her failures.
He did not ask about her qualifications.
Because what we seek ultimately reveals what we worship.
But not the Prince of Peace.
But not the King of Heaven.
But not the One who gives purpose.
The Greek word used here is "ζητεῖς" (zēteis), from "ζητέω" (zēteō), meaning to seek, search for, desire, strive after, pursue with intention.
Jesus was not merely asking for information.
Because God has never been interested in superficial religion.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, God repeatedly calls His people to seek Him.
"You will seek Me and find Me."
"When you seek Me with all your heart." (Jeremiah 29:13)
Because many people seek God the way they seek a spare key.
The man who experienced triumphs and scandals.
"O God, You are my God; earnestly I seek You." (Psalm 63:1)
And perhaps that is what makes this question so uncomfortable.
It cuts through church attendance records.
Many of us have spent years seeking acceptance.
Because every created thing eventually reveals its limitations.
This is why the resurrection account is so breathtaking.
Mary thought she was searching for a dead Savior.
Instead, she encountered a living King.
She was looking for a body.
She found the Author of Life.
Everything changed when Jesus called her name.
That is still what Jesus does.
Because Christianity is not primarily about finding a better version of yourself.
It is about being found by Christ.
The Gospel begins long before we sought Him.
In Genesis, after Adam and Eve sinned, God came into the garden asking:
But because He was initiating redemption.
The God of Scripture is the God who seeks.
The Shepherd who seeks the lost sheep.
The Father who waits for the prodigal son.
The Savior who came "to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10).
Because many readers may feel disqualified.
Yet the Gospel announces astonishing news.
David was marked by adultery and murder.
Mary Magdalene was once tormented by demons.
Not because their sin was small.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message.
The transformed lives of millions prove it.
The question therefore remains before every reader.
If you seek success, eventually you will discover its limits.
If you seek pleasure, eventually it fades.
If you seek approval, eventually it disappoints.
If you seek yourself, eventually you become exhausted.
But if you seek Christ, you find the One who never changes.
The One who heals what shame destroyed.
The One who gives eternal life.
The One who still calls people by name.
Perhaps that is why this question has survived two thousand years.
Because it is not merely a biblical question.
It is the question behind every human story.
And maybe, just maybe, the deeper miracle is that while you have been searching for answers, Jesus has been pursuing you all along.
If this message stirred something inside your soul, do not ignore it.
Your testimony may become the encouragement another struggling believer desperately needs today.
One day every voice, every ambition, every kingdom, every achievement, and every treasure will fade—but the answer you gave to Christ's question will echo forever.
